pack.blurb: Elements, compounds, gases, alloys, glassware and the people who mixed them.

prompts.flavor: Everything that was, is or will be is built from these. Even the things below.
prompts.rules: Any of the 118 elements of the periodic table, by name. British and American spellings both count.

Named after Prometheus, who stole fire from the gods.
So unstable that nobody has ever gathered enough of it to see.
One of four elements named after the same Swedish village, Ytterby.
The rarest naturally occurring element in the Earth's crust. Its name means 'unstable'.

prompts.flavor: Some sour your milk. Some eat through steel. Some wrote the instructions for building you.
prompts.rules: Any acid by its chemical, everyday or old name, or its formula: mineral or organic, strong or weak, including amino, fatty and nucleic acids. Salts, bases and sour foods don't count.

answers.lore: Your stomach makes it. The stomach lining is replaced every few days, partly so it isn't digested too.
Made in greater amounts than any other chemical. Its output was once a measure of a nation's industrial might.
Alchemists called it aqua fortis, strong water, and used it to part silver from gold.
Most of the world's supply is made by a black mould, Aspergillus niger, fed on sugar.
Pure acetic acid freezes at about 17°C, so a chilly laboratory turns it to ice: hence glacial acetic acid.
Long blamed for next-day muscle ache, which it does not in fact cause.
Stretched out, the DNA in a single human cell would reach about 2 metres.
Its name means 'against scurvy', the disease that a lack of it causes.
Weak by a chemist's measure, yet it eats through glass.
Named from the Latin for ant: it was first distilled from a heap of dead ants.
Gives cola its tang.
Named from the Latin for leaf, as it was first taken from spinach.
The white part of bird droppings is mostly uric acid.
A mild antiseptic still used in eyewashes, and an old favourite for killing cockroaches.
Called prussic acid because it was first made, in 1782, from the pigment Prussian blue.
Named after the willow, Salix, whose bark was chewed for pain long before aspirin.
Bayer began selling it as Aspirin in 1899.
Rhubarb leaves are full of it, which is why people eat the stalks and not the leaves.
Named after the Latin for apple, it gives sour sweets their sharpness.
In 1848 Louis Pasteur found that molecules can be left- or right-handed by sorting crystals of its salt with tweezers.
Named after gum benzoin, a tree resin. It keeps soft drinks from spoiling.
Joseph Lister used it to keep surgical wounds free of germs from 1865, founding antiseptic surgery.
Your white blood cells make it to kill germs.
In 1940 George de Hevesy dissolved two Nobel medals in it to hide them from the Nazis. The gold was later recast.
The strongest superacid known. It would eat through glass, so it is kept in Teflon.
Packed into British shells as the explosive lyddite, named after Lydd in Kent.
Named after butter, and to blame for the smell when butter goes rancid.
Its name means 'first fat'. The bacteria that make it in Swiss cheese also blow the holes.
From the Greek for tallow. It hardens candles and soap.
Named after the palm tree. It is the commonest saturated fat in plants and animals.
Makes up most of olive oil.
Named after the laurel. About half of coconut oil is made of it.
Its salt, monosodium glutamate, carries the taste of umami, which Kikunae Ikeda identified in 1908.
First distilled from amber, which the Romans called succinum.
First made from nicotine, but it is a vitamin, better known as niacin.
From the Greek for 'from everywhere', as it turns up in almost every food.
The brain's main calming messenger.
Albert Hofmann turned it into LSD in 1938, and found out what that did in 1943.
Named after the rowan tree, Sorbus, whose berries first gave it up.
The simplest amino acid, and the first found in a comet, in dust brought home by NASA's Stardust.
The reason drinks sweetened with aspartame carry a warning for people with phenylketonuria.
Blamed for sleepiness after turkey dinners, though turkey has no more of it than chicken.
In Jurassic Park the dinosaurs were engineered to need it in their food, so they would die if they escaped.
Named after the ox, Taurus, because it was first found in ox bile, in 1827.
Said per-iodic: an acid of iodine, with nothing to do with the periodic table.
Its salts, the fulminates, explode at a sharp knock, and once fired percussion caps.
Named in 1966 after it dissolved a candle at a Christmas party in George Olah's laboratory.
Named after valerian, the herbal sleep remedy, whose root smells of old socks.
Named after goats, whose smell it shares.
Named after nutmeg, Myristica.
Old rapeseed oil was rich in it, so in the 1970s Canadian breeders made canola, low in it.
Mixed with iron salts, it made the iron gall ink of medieval manuscripts.
Extracted from star anise to make the flu drug Tamiflu.
Cheap and simple, it saves lives by stopping heavy bleeding after injuries and childbirth.
Named for the leaf fall it was thought to cause. It mostly helps plants survive drought.
Found in a fungus that made rice seedlings grow so tall they toppled over.
Gives carmine, the red dye crushed from cochineal insects, its colour.
Adolf von Baeyer made it in 1864. Legend says he named it after a woman called Barbara.
One of the 'forever chemicals', once used to make non-stick pans.
The first amino acid to be discovered, taken from asparagus juice in 1806.
A big part of the smell of sweaty feet.
Found in human skin oil and almost nowhere else, hence its name, from Homo sapiens.
Named from the Latin for cow, as it is found in beef fat and milk.
Named after the scientist James Mead, not the honey drink.
Named after the pomegranate, Punica granatum, whose seed oil is rich in it.
Napalm takes its name from naphthenic and palmitic acids, whose salts thickened it.
Its four carbon atoms form an almost perfect square.
Its three carbon atoms form a triangle, hence the Greek letter delta in its name.
First found in mellite, or honeystone, a rare mineral named for its honey colour.
Named after horses, as it was first found in their urine.
The sweet taste of liquorice root, 30 to 50 times sweeter than sugar.
Once called vitamin B13, though it turned out not to be a vitamin.
Sold as vitamin B15, though it is not a vitamin and no one agrees exactly what it is.
The 21st amino acid, built around selenium instead of sulfur.
The 22nd amino acid, found in some of the microbes that make methane.
Gives the tuberculosis germ its waxy coat, one reason it is so hard to kill.
In the disorder alkaptonuria it builds up in the body and turns urine black when left to stand.
A plant hormone that helps wounds heal, hence its name.
An acid of xenon, a noble gas long thought too aloof to react with anything at all.
A million times stronger than pure sulfuric acid, yet so gentle it can be kept in a glass bottle.
Named after the herb angelica, which legend says an archangel revealed as a cure for the plague.

prompts.flavor: Smaller than anything you will ever see, and stranger. Some are passing straight through you right now.
prompts.rules: Any particle smaller than an atom, elementary or composite, matter or antimatter, including nuclei and hypothetical particles such as the graviton. Atoms, exotic atoms and quasiparticles don't count.

answers.lore: Found by J. J. Thomson in 1897, the first subatomic particle ever discovered.
Named by Ernest Rutherford around 1920. Physicists have waited decades for one to decay and have never seen it happen.
Found by James Chadwick in 1932. Outside a nucleus, a free neutron lasts only about 15 minutes.
Murray Gell-Mann took the name from a line in James Joyce's Finnegans Wake: 'Three quarks for Muster Mark!'
Einstein won his Nobel Prize for showing that light comes in packets, the particles later named photons.
Wolfgang Pauli proposed it in 1930 and fretted that he had predicted a particle nobody could ever detect. It was caught in 1956.
Predicted in 1964 and found at CERN in 2012. Peter Higgs disliked its nickname, the God particle.
The first antiparticle. Paul Dirac's 1928 equation implied it, and it was found in cosmic rays in 1932.
So unexpected that the physicist Isidor Rabi is said to have asked, 'Who ordered that?'
Named because it glues quarks together inside protons and neutrons.
The hypothetical carrier of gravity. One estimate says a detector the mass of Jupiter, near a neutron star, might catch one a decade.
The particle actually caught in 1956, streaming out of a nuclear reactor in South Carolina.
Rutherford's team fired them at gold foil in 1909, and the few that bounced back revealed the atomic nucleus.
An electron, or a positron, flung out of a nucleus as it decays.
The heaviest known elementary particle, about as heavy as an atom of gold. It was found at Fermilab in 1995.
Predicted by Hideki Yukawa in 1935 as the carrier of the force that holds nuclei together, and found in 1947.
Found in 1975, the heaviest lepton is nearly twice as heavy as a proton.
Its discovery in 1974, inside the J/psi particle, was so sudden that physicists call it the November Revolution.
Its odd behaviour gave physicists the idea of 'strangeness', and so led to the strange quark.
Found by two teams at once in 1974. One called it J, the other psi, so it carries both names.
A hypothetical particle that could only travel faster than light. The less energy it had, the faster it would go.
Frank Wilczek named it after a laundry detergent, because it would clean up a problem in physics.
Five quarks bound together. Allowed by theory since 1964, they were finally confirmed at CERN in 2015.
The last of the leptons to be seen directly, at Fermilab in 2000.
Murray Gell-Mann predicted it, and its mass, in 1962. It turned up two years later, just as forecast.
Found at Fermilab in 1977, it revealed the bottom quark.
A leading candidate for dark matter. The rival idea, dim stars and black holes, was given the name MACHO.
A particle that is its own antiparticle, named after Ettore Majorana, the Italian physicist who vanished without trace in 1938.
Proposed in 1973 and confirmed in 2021, by comparing proton collisions at CERN with proton–antiproton collisions at Fermilab.
Hinted at in 2016 by a Hungarian lab studying beryllium-8. Teams in Vietnam and Italy have since seen hints, but it is still unconfirmed.
A magnet with only one pole. On Valentine's Day 1982 a detector at Stanford recorded what looked like one passing through. It was never seen again.
A particle made of pure force: gluons bound to gluons, with no quarks at all. Predicted in the 1970s, it has never been confirmed beyond doubt.
A hypothetical lump of up, down and strange quarks. Before big colliders opened, some feared one could convert the Earth. Safety studies said no.

traps.reason: That covers a whole group of particles. Name one.
Too big: atoms are built from subatomic particles.
Too big: a molecule is built from atoms.
An atom with an electric charge, too big to be subatomic.
A kind of atom, too big to be subatomic.
An exotic atom: two particles orbiting each other like a tiny atom.
A quasiparticle: a ripple in a solid that behaves like a particle, not a particle in its own right.
Two electrons paired across hundreds of atoms in a superconductor: far bigger than an atom.
A state of matter, a soup of free quarks and gluons, not a particle.
A dead star, made almost entirely of neutrons.
Matter built from the mirror images of ordinary particles. Name one of those.
Nobody knows yet what it is made of. Name a candidate particle.
A stream of particles. Name the particle.
An amount, not a particle.
A region where an electron is likely to be found, not a particle.
In string theory particles are tiny vibrating strings, but a string itself is not a particle.
A force, not a particle. Name the particle that carries it.
The field, not the particle. Name the particle that goes with it.
A property of particles, not a particle.
Massive compact halo objects are things like dim stars and black holes, not particles.
Fiction: tiny life forms from Star Wars.
Fiction: Ant-Man's shrinking particles, from Marvel.
Fiction: made-up particles from Star Trek.
Fiction: a made-up material, not a particle.
No such thing: its mirror image is the same kind of particle.
A state of matter, not a particle.
Ordinary stuff, made of particles. Name one of them.
Whatever is speeding up the universe's expansion. As far as anyone knows, it is not a particle.
An atom of antimatter, too big to be subatomic.

prompts.flavor: Two metals melted into one. Neither was asked, and neither can ever leave.
prompts.rules: Any mixture of a metal with other elements, by its common or trade name.

answers.lore: Melts at about 70 degrees. The classic chemists' prank is a teaspoon cast from it, which vanishes into a hot cup of tea as the victim stirs.
Plato said it gleamed on the walls of Atlantis, second only to gold. Ingots found in a 2,600-year-old wreck off Sicily suggest it was a kind of brass.

traps.reason: That is a pure element. An alloy is a blend of a metal with something else.

prompts.text: Name a piece of laboratory equipment.
prompts.flavor: Glass, flame and patience. Wear the goggles. They are not there for the things you can see.
prompts.rules: Any apparatus, glassware, instrument or safety gear found in a science lab.

answers.lore: Three glass bulbs stacked like a snowman, invented by a Dutch pharmacist around 1844. It makes gas on demand and stops by itself when you close the tap.
Glassware shaped like a pistol, for drying samples in boiling vapour. Its namesake's celebrated "defence enzymes" turned out not to exist.

traps.reason: In the room, perhaps, but not what we would call lab equipment.
Which one? Name the piece.

prompts.flavor: Half of them were burned, poisoned or blown up by their own work. They wrote it down first.
prompts.rules: Anyone famous for their work in chemistry, from the alchemists onward. Surnames are fine.

answers.lore: Boiled down thousands of litres of urine in 1669, looking for gold. He found a white glow in the dark instead, and became the first person to discover an element.
Sydney-born and profoundly deaf from his teens, he shared the 1975 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for working out how enzymes build molecules in three dimensions.
A perfume-maker named on a Babylonian clay tablet from about 1200 BC. She distilled and filtered her scents, and is the first chemist whose name we know.

traps.reason: A great scientist, but not remembered for chemistry.
Name a chemist, by name. Jesse never did finish the course.

prompts.flavor: You cannot see most of them. Several are in the room with you. One of them is waiting.
prompts.rules: Any substance that is a gas at room temperature, by its name or formula, plus well-known mixtures and anything commonly called a gas.

answers.lore: Helium's opposite: five times heavier than air, so a breath of it drops your voice into the cellar. It is also the strongest greenhouse gas known.
So reactive it sets fire to glass, sand and asbestos. When a tonne of it spilled in the 1950s it burned through 30 cm of concrete and a metre of gravel.

traps.reason: A liquid at room temperature, even if its fumes get about.
Which one? Name the gas.
A solid at room temperature.

prompts.text: Name a plastic or other polymer.
prompts.flavor: Long chains, patiently linked. Nothing we make lasts longer. It will be here after us.
prompts.rules: Any plastic, synthetic fibre, rubber or natural polymer, by its chemical, common or brand name.

answers.lore: "Milk stone": a plastic made from milk protein and formaldehyde in the 1890s. For decades it was the world's buttons, knitting needles and fountain pens.
The first man-made plastic, shown by Alexander Parkes at London's 1862 exhibition. It was cellulose nitrate, flammable and prone to cracking, and his company went broke.

traps.reason: Not a polymer: it is not built from long chains of repeating units.
Which one? Name the plastic or polymer.

prompts.text: Name a family of organic compounds or a functional group.
prompts.flavor: Carbon will bond with almost anything. It is the least particular of the elements, and the busiest.
prompts.rules: Any class of carbon compound or the group of atoms that defines one, such as the family whose simplest member is methane.

answers.lore: Its simplest member, thioacetone, may be the worst smell known. An attempt to make it in Freiburg in 1889 caused vomiting and panic across the city.
Rings of carbon and oxygen that sit on a metal ion like a crown on a head. Charles Pedersen found them by accident in 1961 and won a Nobel Prize for it.

traps.reason: That is a single compound. Name the family it belongs to, or the group that defines it.
Which one? Name the family or the group.
That belongs to inorganic chemistry.
